lessons.title: Bank Imposter Scam
lessons.summary: Fake bank calls demanding your PIN
lessons.body: They say "Account frozen - verify now!" from unknown numbers. Real banks never call asking for your PIN or password.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Call your real bank using the number on your card!

lessons.title: Prize Scam
lessons.body: Callers claim you won a prize but need to pay fees first. Real prizes are free - no payment required!
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → If it sounds too good to be true, it is!

lessons.title: Grandparent Scam
lessons.body: Call from unknown number saying "I'm in jail - send gift cards now!" They pretend to be your grandkid.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Call your real grandkid directly to verify!

lessons.title: Tech Support Scam
lessons.body: Callers claim your computer is hacked and need remote access. Real tech support never calls you first.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Never give remote access to unknown callers!

lessons.title: IRS Tax Scam
lessons.body: Callers claim you owe back taxes and must pay immediately or face arrest. The real IRS never calls demanding immediate payment.
danger_signs: Asks for gift cards or wire transfer
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → The IRS sends letters, not threatening calls!

lessons.title: Social Security Scam
lessons.body: Callers claim your Social Security number is suspended due to suspicious activity. Real SSA never calls about this.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Contact Social Security directly if concerned!

lessons.title: Romance Scam
lessons.summary: Online dating fraud and fake relationships
lessons.body: Scammers create fake profiles, build trust, then ask for money for emergencies. Real relationships don't ask for money.
danger_signs: Asks for money early in relationship
Has excuses to never meet in person
lessons.safe_action: Stop contact → Never send money to someone you haven't met!

lessons.title: Phishing Email Scam
lessons.summary: Fake emails trying to steal your info
lessons.body: Emails that look real but are fake, asking you to click links or provide passwords. Real companies don't email asking for passwords.
danger_signs: Asks for password or account info
lessons.safe_action: Delete email → Never click links in suspicious emails!

lessons.title: Medicare Scam
lessons.summary: Fake Medicare calls asking for card info
lessons.body: Callers claim to be from Medicare and need your card number to send a new card. Real Medicare never calls asking for your card number.
danger_signs: Claims you need a new card
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Medicare sends cards by mail, never calls!

lessons.title: Utility Scam
lessons.summary: "Your power will be shut off" fake calls
lessons.body: Callers claim your utility bill is overdue and power will be shut off unless you pay now. Real utilities send written notices first.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Call your utility company directly to verify!

lessons.title: Sweepstakes Scam
lessons.body: Callers claim you won a sweepstakes but need to pay taxes or fees first. Real sweepstakes never require payment to claim prizes.
danger_signs: Asks for payment to claim prize
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Real prizes are free, no fees required!

lessons.title: Fake Gift Scam
lessons.summary: Unrequested package with QR code to steal your card info
lessons.body: A package arrives claiming to be a gift. A note says to scan a QR code to find out who sent it. The QR code takes you to a fake site that asks for your credit card to "verify" or "claim" the gift. Real senders never need your card info to tell you who gave a gift.
danger_signs: Asks you to scan a QR code
QR leads to site asking for card info
lessons.safe_action: Don't scan the QR → Look up the company on the package yourself. Real senders don't need your card to reveal who sent a gift!

lessons.title: Pretend Charge Scam
lessons.summary: Fake approval of a big purchase, then "dispute" to steal your card
lessons.body: You get a call, text, or email saying a large purchase was approved (e.g. an iPhone for $1500). They ask if you want to dispute it, then say they need your card number to "verify" or "cancel" the charge. Real banks never ask for your full card details over the phone to dispute a charge.
danger_signs: Claims a large purchase you didn't make was approved
Offers to help you "dispute" the charge
Asks for card number or details to "verify"
Pressure to act before the charge posts
lessons.safe_action: Hang up → Call your bank directly using the number on your card or statement. Never give card info to someone who contacted you!

lessons.title: It's OK to Hang Up
lessons.summary: Easiest way to avoid fraud is to hang up
lessons.body: Scammers pressure you not to hang up—they create urgency or threaten consequences if you disconnect. Real banks and companies are fine with you calling back. The easiest way to avoid fraud is to hang up and call the real number yourself.
danger_signs: Threats or urgency if you disconnect
Says you can't call back or will lose your chance
Real companies never pressure you to stay on the line
lessons.safe_action: Hang up anytime → Look up the real number and call back. Real banks and businesses are fine with it!

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a bank call is a scam?

options.text: Says they're calling from your local branch
Asks for your PIN or password
Calls from a known bank number

quizQuestions.explanation: Real banks NEVER call asking for your PIN or password. This is the #1 red flag.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger if you give your PIN to a scammer?

options.text: They can steal all your money
Nothing, PINs are safe to share
You'll get more spam calls

quizQuestions.explanation: Your PIN gives full access to your account. Scammers can drain your account immediately.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when a caller claims your bank account is frozen?

options.text: Hang up & call your bank directly
Stay on the line while they "verify" your account
Give them your account info to verify

quizQuestions.explanation: Always hang up and call your bank using the number on your card. Never trust incoming calls.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a prize call is a scam?

options.text: Asks you to pay fees upfront
Congratulates you on winning
Asks for your mailing address

quizQuestions.explanation: Real prizes are FREE. If they ask for payment, it's always a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of paying "processing fees" for a prize?

options.text: Your prize will be delayed
You'll owe taxes on the prize
You lose money, no prize exists

quizQuestions.explanation: There is no prize. Scammers take your money and disappear. You'll never see a prize.

quizQuestions.question: What should you say when someone claims you won a prize?

options.text: Ask for more details about the prize
Pay a fee to "check" if you won
Hang up immediately

quizQuestions.explanation: If it sounds too good to be true, it is. Hang up - real prizes don't require payment.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a "grandkid in trouble" call is a scam?

options.text: Voice sounds like your grandkid
Knows your grandkid's name
Call from unknown number

quizQuestions.explanation: Scammers use unknown numbers and won't let you verify. Real emergencies come from known numbers.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of sending gift cards to a "grandkid in jail"?

options.text: Money is lost, can't be recovered
They'll ask for more money
You'll face legal trouble

quizQuestions.explanation: Gift cards are untraceable. Once sent, the money is gone forever and can't be recovered.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do if someone claims to be your grandkid in trouble?

options.text: Hang up & call your grandkid directly
Send money immediately to help
Send a small amount to verify it's really them

quizQuestions.explanation: Always verify by calling your grandkid directly on their known number. Real emergencies can wait for verification.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a tech support call is a scam?

options.text: They called you first
Knows what computer you have
Uses a real company name

quizQuestions.explanation: Real tech support NEVER calls you first. If they call unsolicited, it's always a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of giving remote access to your computer?

options.text: Your computer will run slower
They can steal all your files and passwords
You'll get computer viruses

quizQuestions.explanation: Remote access gives them full control. They can steal passwords, files, and install malware.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when someone claims your computer is hacked?

options.text: Follow their instructions to open a website
Hang up immediately
Let them access your computer to fix it

quizQuestions.explanation: Never give remote access to unknown callers. Hang up - real tech support doesn't call you.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates an IRS call is a scam?

options.text: Says you may be due a refund
Threatens immediate arrest
Sends a letter first before calling

quizQuestions.explanation: The real IRS NEVER threatens arrest over the phone. They send letters first, not threatening calls.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger if you pay "back taxes" via gift cards?

options.text: You'll be audited
You'll owe late fees
Money is stolen, IRS never gets it

quizQuestions.explanation: The IRS never accepts gift cards. Your money goes to scammers and you still owe real taxes.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when someone claims to be from the IRS demanding payment?

options.text: Ask them to verify their identity
Pay immediately to avoid arrest
Hang up - IRS sends letters, not calls

quizQuestions.explanation: The IRS sends letters by mail, not threatening phone calls. Hang up and ignore the call.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a Social Security call is a scam?

options.text: Talks about your benefits
Says they're from the Social Security office
Claims your SSN is suspended

quizQuestions.explanation: Social Security numbers CANNOT be suspended. This is always a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of giving your SSN to a scammer?

options.text: More spam calls
They can steal your identity
You'll lose your benefits

quizQuestions.explanation: Your SSN can be used to open accounts, file taxes, and commit identity theft in your name.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do if someone claims your Social Security number is suspended?

options.text: Provide your SSN to verify
Hang up - SSNs can't be suspended
Stay on the line so they can "unsuspend" it

quizQuestions.explanation: SSNs cannot be suspended. Hang up immediately - this is always a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates an online romance is a scam?

options.text: Talks to you every day
Asks for money early in relationship
Sends photos of themselves

quizQuestions.explanation: Real relationships don't ask for money. If they ask early on, it's a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of sending money to someone you've never met?

options.text: Money is lost, relationship is fake
The relationship will end
They'll ask for more money

quizQuestions.explanation: You'll lose your money and the "relationship" is fake. They'll disappear once you stop paying.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do if someone online asks for money?

options.text: Stop contact immediately
Send money to help while you verify
Send money to help them

quizQuestions.explanation: Never send money to someone you haven't met. Real relationships don't ask for money.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates an email is a phishing scam?

options.text: Asks for your password
Has a company logo
Looks professional

quizQuestions.explanation: Real companies NEVER email asking for passwords. This is always a phishing scam.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of clicking links in phishing emails?

options.text: More emails go to spam
Your computer slows down
Scammers can hack your account

quizQuestions.explanation: Fake login pages steal your password, giving scammers full access to your account.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do with a suspicious email asking for your password?

options.text: Click the link to verify
Click the link to check if it's real
Delete the email immediately

quizQuestions.explanation: Never click links or reply. Delete suspicious emails - real companies don't email for passwords.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a Medicare call is a scam?

options.text: Says they're from Medicare
Talks about your benefits
Asks for your Medicare card number

quizQuestions.explanation: Real Medicare NEVER calls asking for your card number. They send cards by mail.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of giving your Medicare card number to a scammer?

options.text: They can commit medical fraud in your name
More scam calls
You'll lose your benefits

quizQuestions.explanation: Scammers can use your Medicare number to bill for fake services, causing medical fraud.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when someone calls claiming to be from Medicare?

options.text: Hang up - Medicare sends mail, not calls
Give them your Medicare card number
Ask them to verify their identity

quizQuestions.explanation: Medicare sends information by mail, not phone calls. Hang up immediately.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a utility call is a scam?

options.text: Asks for your account number
Threatens immediate shutoff
Says your bill is overdue

quizQuestions.explanation: Real utilities send written notices first. Immediate shutoff threats are always scams.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of paying utility bills with gift cards?

options.text: Money is stolen, bill never paid
You'll owe late fees
Your service will be cut off

quizQuestions.explanation: Utilities don't accept gift cards. Your money goes to scammers and your real bill remains unpaid.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when someone threatens to shut off your utilities?

options.text: Hang up & call your utility directly
Give them your account to verify
Pay immediately with gift cards

quizQuestions.explanation: Always hang up and call your utility company directly using the number on your bill.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a sweepstakes call is a scam?

options.text: You never entered the contest
Congratulates you on winning
Asks for your contact information

quizQuestions.explanation: You can't win contests you never entered. This is always a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of paying "taxes" to claim a sweepstakes prize?

options.text: You'll owe tax penalties
Your prize will be delayed
You lose money, no prize exists

quizQuestions.explanation: There is no prize. Real sweepstakes never require payment. You'll lose your money.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when someone claims you won a sweepstakes?

options.text: Pay the taxes to claim your prize
Pay a fee to "check" if you won
Hang up - real prizes are free

quizQuestions.explanation: Real prizes are free with no fees. Hang up immediately - this is always a scam.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a "gift" package might be a scam?

options.text: Has a shipping label on it
You weren't expecting a package
Asks you to scan a QR code to find out who sent it

quizQuestions.explanation: Real senders don't need you to scan a QR code to reveal who they are. A QR code that "reveals the sender" is often a trap to steal your card info.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of scanning a QR code on an unrequested gift package?

options.text: The site can steal your credit card info
You'll get more spam
Your phone might get a virus

quizQuestions.explanation: Fake gift scams send you to a site that asks for your card to "verify" or "claim" the gift. They're after your payment info.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when you get an unrequested package that says to scan a QR code to find the sender?

options.text: Don't scan it - look up the company yourself if curious
Scan the QR code to see who sent it
Call the number on the package

quizQuestions.explanation: Never scan QR codes on unsolicited packages. Real senders don't need your card to tell you who gave a gift.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a "charge dispute" call or message is a scam?

options.text: Asks for your card number to "verify" or cancel the charge
Says a purchase was approved
Mentions a large purchase amount

quizQuestions.explanation: Real banks never ask for your full card number over the phone to dispute a charge. They already have your info.

quizQuestions.question: What's the danger of giving your card info to someone who says a big charge was approved?

options.text: The charge will stay on your account
They can use your card for fraud
Your account might be frozen

quizQuestions.explanation: Scammers use the "dispute" story to get your card details. Once they have them, they can make real charges.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do when someone says a large purchase was approved on your card?

options.text: Let them "dispute" it for you
Hang up and call your bank directly with the number on your card
Give them your card number to verify

quizQuestions.explanation: Always call your bank yourself using the number on your card or statement. Never give card info to someone who contacted you.

quizQuestions.question: What indicates a caller might be a scammer?

options.text: They say the name of a real bank
They pressure you not to hang up
They give you a case number

quizQuestions.explanation: Real companies don't pressure you to stay on the line. Scammers create urgency so you don't hang up and verify.

quizQuestions.question: Why do scammers pressure you not to hang up?

options.text: Their company policy requires it
They're worried about a bad connection
So you don't have time to verify or call the real company

quizQuestions.explanation: If you hang up and call the real number yourself, the scam fails. So they keep you on the line with urgency or threats.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do if a caller won't let you hang up to verify?

options.text: Ask to speak to a supervisor
Stay on the line to hear them out
Hang up anyway - real companies are fine with you calling back

quizQuestions.explanation: You can hang up anytime. Look up the real number and call back. Real banks and businesses are fine with it.
